title: A library, not a book
hook: Protestants have 66 books, Catholics 73, Orthodox a few more

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small sabbath, and your line: stop. it still counts. Now the second half of this stretch: scripture.

Pick up a Bible. It looks like one book: one cover, one spine, thin pages, tiny print. Now open the contents page. Genesis. Exodus. Psalms. Proverbs. Isaiah. Matthew. Romans. Revelation. Dozens of titles, written over more than a thousand years, by many different hands, in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek. Poetry, law, history, letters, songs, wild visions of the end of the world. It isn't a book at all. It's a library. Even the word Bible says so: Greek ta biblia, the books. Plural. Put two Bibles side by side, and a question appears: who decided which books go in?
screen: `ONE COVER, DOZENS OF TITLES.` → `THREE LANGUAGES, A THOUSAND YEARS.` → `TA BIBLIA: THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Canon. From the Greek kanon, a straight reed, a measuring rod, a rule. The canon is the list of books a church measures as scripture, and the lists aren't all the same. Protestant Bibles have sixty-six books: thirty-nine in the Old Testament, twenty-seven in the New. Catholic Bibles have seventy-three, adding seven books to the Old Testament, among them Tobit, Judith, Wisdom and the two books of Maccabees, plus extra parts of Esther and Daniel. Catholics call these deuterocanonical, the second canon; Protestants often call them the Apocrypha. Orthodox Bibles have a few more still, such as a third book of Maccabees and a Psalm 151. And the Ethiopian Orthodox Church has the broadest canon of all, including the book of Enoch. A surprise: the King James Bible of 1611 printed the Apocrypha, between the two testaments. Many later printings left it out. What almost everyone shares is the New Testament: the same twenty-seven books, in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles alike. The earliest list that matches those twenty-seven exactly comes from a letter by a bishop, Athanasius, in 367. The Jewish Bible, the Tanakh, has the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, in a different order and counted as twenty-four. Christians hold these differences without pretending they don't exist, but they tend to agree on what the library is for. The writers disagree, argue, grieve and sing, and Christians hear them all telling one long story: God and people, from a garden to a city. The book itself says, "All scripture is given by inspiration of God."
screen: `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `66, 73, AND A FEW MORE.` · `THE SAME 27 IN THE NEW.` · `MANY VOICES, ONE STORY.`

segments.voice: If there's a Bible near you, open it to the contents page; if not, picture a long bookshelf. Let the titles go by slowly, stories, then laws, histories, songs and wisdom, prophets, four Gospels, letters, and a vision at the end, and let one you've never read, or never heard of, catch your eye. If you pray, ask for curiosity; if you don't, simply notice what you're curious about.
Canon. From the Greek for measuring rod. The list of books a church accepts as scripture.
Your line: many voices, one story. The shelves differ a little; the library is one. See you tomorrow.
